look_here_first: BARNYARDGRASS: look first at a clean and intact grass BLADE–SHEATH junction: there is NO true ligule (neither projecting membrane nor fringe) and NO auricles. Our new licensed Harry Rose photo demonstrates this negative character, absent from older gallery. Next trace the crowded flowering panicle and its side branches; find mature true spikelets (typically 2.5–4 mm) with variable lower sterile-lemma awns. The new real author-labelled spikelet photograph teaches multiple florets as botanically distinct from separate spikelets. IMPORTANT: native E. muricata shares the absent ligule; never identify introduced E. crus-galli from a distant head alone. To distinguish it, examine the abruptly delimited thin terminal margin and short hair line on the mature upper fertile lemma at ~25–40x.

morphology_keys.life_cycle: Annual, warm-season grass, often stout 0.3–1.2 m in Texas descriptions; grows in moist/disturbed soil, ditches, trails and edges.
best_field_traits: ABSENT leaf ligule and auricles; hair at nearby collar cannot substitute.
Smooth/glabrous sheaths, rather broad flat blades with pale conspicuous midvein; lower stem may be reddish.
Branching often erect to nodding terminal panicle with dense clusters of spikelets; flowering branch rachis frequently rough or bristly.
Spikelets around 2.5–4 mm long; lower fertile structures may be awnless or awned, even varying along one branch.
Mature upper fertile lemma hard body abruptly separated from thin membranous tip by line of minute hairs; inspect at ~25×.
crew_field_check: LOOK AT COLLAR: confirm no true ligule or auricles (not shown by original stored picture).
LOOK AT PANICLE: find branching axis and compact clustered spikelets (original photo markers show these).
LOOK UNDER MICROSCOPE: where E. muricata is possible, identify the abrupt membranous fertile lemma tip and line of minute hairs; if invisible leave Echinochloa sp.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: High resolution true collar close-up showing a blade/sheath junction without projecting ligule or auricles; include millimeter reference.
Whole robust plant including lower reddish/green sheaths and basal rooted tuft.
One mature spikelet beside 1-mm ruler, glumes and variable lower sterile-lemma awns visible.
25–40× comparison of mature fertile upper lemma TIP and line of minute hairs of E. crus-galli versus E. muricata; include palea tip.
Rachis node macro of bristle-like hairs with clear anatomical scale; NOT a substitute for final species call.
Actually inspect all external photos before selecting additional arrows; archive rights-clean files if accepted for public gallery.
diagnostic_photo_sequence_20261022: 1. START at whole plant: inspect source-labelled rooted rosette/young shoot (prior Polish photo) and mature stand (previous Maui photo).
2. Show TRUE leaf collar, at blade/sheath junction (Harry Rose 'ligule1'): no projecting flap nor hairy ligule. Absence must be proven on intact clean leaf; adjacent sparse hairs are not a ligule.
3. Follow full terminal PANICLE from main axis into lateral spikelet-rich branches. Existing locally stored Mark Marathon photo has three actually reviewed broad arrows.
4. Look at actual lower sterile lemma awn variability (Matt Lavin photo). Awn length is NOT sole species separator within Echinochloa.
5. Inspect true spikelet anatomy in original author-annotated Harry Rose actual macro (2-flowered, usually 2.5–4 mm in treatment). The body of one spikelet is NOT one panicle branch.
6. Inspect mature spikelets in second Harry Rose image; identify mature fertile upper lemma and lower sterile units, though individual pixel labels beyond source not asserted.

7. Compare DIFFERENT SPECIES Digitaria ciliaris photo: its flowering branches are fingers with paired one-flowered units and the plant has an actual membranous ligule (not visible in this comparison photo).

8. Escalate E. crus-galli versus native E. muricata candidates to macro: photograph several attached ripe upper fertile lemmas with basal body and thin distal tip, documenting a real line of minute hairs with 0.5–1 mm bar at 25–40x. If unresolved, label Echinochloa sp.

comparisons.key_distinctions: NO ligule helps distinguish Echinochloa from Digitaria ciliaris and Panicum capillare, but NOT E. crus-galli from E. muricata/colona/walteri. Species-level E. crus-galli is supported by a mature fertile lemma with abruptly delimited thin tip and tiny hairline; E. muricata lacks that demarcation. E. colona generally has smaller, less bristly short panicle branches; E. walteri has often hairy leaf sheaths. These alone are insufficient for assured species calls.

detailed_pairs.look_here_first: Also has NO true ligule and may have a near-identical panicle with variable awns. Some differences in rachis bristles or spikelet hairs are only suggestive and unreliable across populations. CONFIRM several fully mature florets at ~25–40×: E. crus-galli upper fertile lemma has a hardened body that ends abruptly at a thin membranous tip, divided by a tiny line of hairs; E. muricata lacks this sharp demarcation and hair line. Compare the palea tip too.
detailed_pairs.warning: Avoid a native-vs-introduced decision from one seedhead photograph. Local range claims for E. muricata not established in this pass.

detailed_pairs.look_here_first: Also without ligule, but typically smaller/less bristly short-branch panicles, often several short racemes, smaller ~2–3 mm awnless spikelets, and sometimes purplish banding on blades. These clues overlap; check mature anatomy.
detailed_pairs.warning: Color bands and awn absence are not stand-alone identifications.

detailed_pairs.look_here_first: Wetland species also lacking a ligule; much hairier coarse basal leaf sheaths and long awns are useful clues, but confirm mature fertile lemma (no E. crus-galli-type line of hairs beneath the tip).
detailed_pairs.warning: Hairiness varies and does not certify a species. Verify occurrence separately.

detailed_pairs.look_here_first: Thin, extremely open floating/tumbling panicle and true ligule of hairs, unlike typically stout relatively densely clustered Echinochloa branches and absent ligule.
detailed_pairs.warning: Do not conflate with genus Digitaria cognata, commonly called fall witchgrass.

detailed_pairs.look_here_first: Several nearly fingerlike one-sided racemes with paired spikelets, and a definite MEMBRANOUS ligule at the leaf collar.
detailed_pairs.warning: Both are disturbed-site warm-season grasses; head silhouette alone is insufficient.

visual_comparison.title: Barnyardgrass — entire rosette → ACTUAL absent ligule → crowded branching panicle → mature paired floral units
visual_comparison.subtitle: Credited photograph of missing collar structure, author-annotated and mature real spikelets, plus original habit/branching references and one separate crabgrass look-alike. E. muricata needs a microscope-level fertile-lemma tip comparison.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: NO LIGULE at true blade–sheath junction, broad sheaths/branched head, crowded awnless-or-awned spikelets. Barnyardgrass vs native rough barnyardgrass cannot be decided from absent ligule alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Barnyardgrass — three checks before deciding
steps: START at the actual flowering plant and locally archived panicle view: identify the branched axis and crowded spikelets. Existing arrows mark only these gross structures.
OPEN THE INNER COLLAR: the credited Commons close-up explicitly documents ABSENCE of a ligule; a smooth blade-sheath seam is not a short ligule. This photo is remotely linked, not a stored JPEG.
CHECK AWNS: inspect the actual photographed awn-bearing spikelet; rye-like long awns and branch density alone cannot distinguish barnyardgrass.

VIEW THE PHOTOGRAPHER-ANNOTATED SPIKELET then the mature spikelet photograph. These external source images introduce lower sterile versus hardened fertile flowering parts, but the microscope-level apical characters have not been independently verified here.

DISTINGUISH E. muricata: obtain the SAME taxon-vouchered Texas ripe spikelet in focus at 20–40x to examine the fertile lemma tip and minute hairline; if not resolved use Echinochloa sp., not a confident E. crus-galli determination.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: A species-name image from Commons is a taxon-labelled reference, not independent anatomical verification; use microscope for close E. crus-galli / E. muricata calls.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Only one of seven species photo entries is physically stored in this GitHub species folder. True absent-ligule and annotated-spikelet photos are external and must not count as locally archived or finished microscope anatomy.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: START AT LEAF COLLAR: Echinochloa has NO true ligule (no membrane or hair fringe) and no auricles. Next check the coarse terminal branched panicle with densely clustered spikelets and often bristly axis. Awn length, purple color and degree of bristliness vary and DO NOT separate E. crus-galli from native E. muricata. Confirm a mature fertile upper lemma with abruptly membranous tip and line of minute hairs under ~25× before naming a closely similar species.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: NO ligule helps distinguish Echinochloa from Digitaria ciliaris and Panicum capillare, but NOT E. crus-galli from E. muricata/colona/walteri. Species-level E. crus-galli is supported by a mature fertile lemma with abruptly delimited thin tip and tiny hairline; E. muricata lacks that demarcation. E. colona generally has smaller, less bristly short panicle branches; E. walteri has often hairy leaf sheaths. These alone are insufficient for assured species calls.
